923a0df786:
This chapter is the map for the rest of the guide. It covers:

  • the exam facts;
  • the eight domains, with every sub-objective and its weight;
  • the three official sample questions, worked through;
  • a table that sends each objective to the chapter that teaches it;
  • two study plans (six weeks and three weeks), weighted by domain percentage, with the companion folders to run each week;
  • how to use the companion code;
  • how to read the "check the docs" markers;
  • the current model lineup;
  • a method for scenario questions, with the distractor families that recur across the domains.
73a668b301: Source and its limits: the numbers here come from the official CCDV-F exam guide v1.0, July 2026. Anthropic revises exam guides. Before you book, open the current official guide and compare the item count, time, passing score, domain list and weights against the tables below. If they differ, the official guide wins, and you should adjust the study plan percentages to match.
43b6a31119:
What the numbers mean in practice. 120 minutes for 53 items is generous for a careful reader. It's tight for someone who re-reads every option three times. Budget 90 seconds for a first pass on each item, and flag anything that takes longer. Keep 25 minutes at the end for flagged items.

Scenario stems in this exam often run four or five sentences. The deciding fact is usually a single constraint word in the last sentence ("overnight", "untrusted", "across several applications", "must never"). Read the final sentence first, then the stem. It saves time.
a767e2b27e:
Scaled scores. A scaled score maps your raw result onto a fixed range. That lets different forms of the exam, with slightly different difficulty, share one passing mark. So 720 is not a fixed percentage of correct answers.

Treat "about three quarters correct, with no domain collapsed" as a working target. Don't try to compute a minimum number of correct items. The official guide does not publish per-domain cut scores. The domain weights only tell you how many items to expect from each domain.
c485003f21:
Expected items per domain. Multiply each weight by 53 and you get the expected number of items. The rounding matters at the bottom of the list. Domain 4 at 2.6% is one or two items. Domain 3 at 3.1% is one or two. Domain 2 at 33.1% is seventeen or eighteen.

One weak spot in Domain 2 (say, API mechanics) costs more than ignoring Domains 3 and 4 entirely. That doesn't mean you can skip Claude Code. Claude Code content also turns up inside Domain 2 (application design across surfaces, configuration management) and Domain 7 (hooks). So the material in chapter 11 is worth more than its 3.1% suggests.
87c52fc1e4: The table lists every sub-objective in the official guide. For each one it gives the weight as a share of the whole exam, the expected number of items (weight times 53), and the topics the guide names. Every topic in the right-hand column is taught somewhere in chapters 01 to 23. Section 04 gives the mapping.
788e09aaf9:
Three observations shape the study plan.

First, the four largest sub-objectives are all engineering topics, not "AI" ones: 2.5 application design (8.6%), 2.4 software engineering foundations (7.4%), 2.3 API mechanics (6.8%) and 5.2 technical fundamentals (6.1%). Together they make up 28.9% of the exam. That's nearly as much as Domains 6, 7 and 8 combined (29.7%).

An experienced backend engineer has a head start here. But the questions are framed through Claude:

  • REST becomes "the SDK is a REST wrapper, so what does a 529 mean";
  • async becomes "run three guardrail calls concurrently";
  • version control becomes "pin the model snapshot and version the prompt with the code".
f0804a06d4: Second, the security domain is only 8.1%. Yet security reasoning shows up as the deciding factor in questions filed under other domains: tool approval patterns (8.1), hooks for deterministic actions (1.2), content boundaries (2.5), input sanitisation (6.2). Sample question 2 below is an example. Chapters 19 and 20 pay off well beyond their nominal weight.
791ecfcd63: Third, the smallest items (7.3 hooks at 1.0%, 7.4 identity at 1.6%) are cheap to learn. The right answer is usually one idea. A hook is deterministic code that runs regardless of what the model decides. A key belongs in a secret store or environment variable scoped to one workload, never in a prompt, a CLAUDE.md or a repository.
644ecb4843:
The official guide publishes three sample questions. The versions below restate each scenario in this guide's words, with four options of the kind the exam uses. The correct answer and its reasoning follow the guide.

The value of working them lies less in the answers than in the reasoning pattern. In each one, a single phrase in the stem eliminates three options.
93f2e60c9d:
Two phrases decide it. The results are read the next morning, so no user is waiting and latency within the day is irrelevant. And cost should be as low as possible.

The Batch API is priced at 50% of the standard rate. It processes asynchronously within 24 hours (most batches finish much sooner) and keys each result by your custom_id.

Option A pays full price and has to manage rate limits itself. Streaming helps a waiting human see tokens early; it does nothing for a back-office job. Option C buys speed nobody asked for, at a higher price. Option D is the over-engineering distractor: Claude cannot be fine-tuned through the API for this, and running your own model adds cost and operations.

You can combine prompt caching on the shared instructions with batching to lower cost further. Chapter 07 covers batch design, result handling and the realtime-vs-batch decision. Chapter 15 covers the cost arithmetic.
bbb68c4cbf:
This is indirect prompt injection: instructions arrive through data the agent reads, not from the user. No single measure removes it, so the right answer is layered:

  • The content is marked and treated as data: delimited, labelled as untrusted, never concatenated into the system prompt.
  • The blast radius is limited. A research agent doesn't need an unrestricted email tool. If it does need one, a hook or human approval decides whether a send happens, and that works whatever the model was persuaded to do.
  • Guardrails screen inputs and outputs.

Option A is a real mitigation, but only a probabilistic one. It's the classic distractor: a prompt instruction offered where a deterministic control is needed. Option C has the same flaw. Option D removes markup, not the instruction, which is plain text.

Chapter 19 covers injection and layering. Chapter 20 covers hooks. Chapter 21 covers approval patterns for tools.
968b50378e:
The deciding phrases are several applications and write once, maintain in one place. MCP is the standard way to package a capability (tools, resources, prompts) so that any MCP client can use it. Claude Code, Claude Desktop and the Agent SDK all act as MCP clients.

Option A works for one application and duplicates the integration three times.

Option C misreads what Skills are for. A Skill packages instructions and know-how: procedures, scripts, reference material loaded on demand. It is not a live connection to a system. A Skill can tell Claude how to use the inventory tools well, but the access itself comes from a tool or MCP server.

Option D asks the model to perform HTTP itself, which it can't do without a tool. It also puts authentication and validation in the wrong place.

Chapter 22 covers MCP server authoring and deployment. Chapter 23 covers when to choose a custom tool, a Skill, an MCP server or a built-in tool.
1178470071: The pattern across all three is the same. Identify the constraint. Map it to the mechanism Anthropic designed for that constraint. Then distrust two kinds of option: those that over-engineer (fine-tuning, a new platform), and those that rely on the model's good behaviour for something that has to be guaranteed. Section 08 turns this into a method.
0ba69a7117: The guide has one primary chapter per objective, or per pair of small objectives. Some topics are owned by one chapter and used by others. The "also" column lists where a topic is applied in a way the exam may test. Chapters 24 to 26 are planned and marked as such.
6dcc7b39f0: The chapters are numbered in the order of the official guide, which starts with agents. That isn't the best order to learn in, because agents are built out of Messages API calls, tools and context management. The recommended order puts the foundations first and then follows the weights.
f12573de52: Foundations (read first, in this order): 05, 13, 14. First the request/response anatomy, stop reasons and statelessness (05). Then what a token is, and how sampling and thinking work (13). Then the HTTP, SSE and SDK layer underneath (14). Nearly every later chapter assumes these.
0022b968c2: Tools and agents: 21, 01, 02, 03, 22, 23. Tool implementation comes before agents, because an agent is a loop around tool calls. Then architecture, construction and patterns. Then MCP and the customization trade-offs.
e4fe0aa8fd: If you prefer the guide order (01 to 23), that works too. The chapters cross-reference each other, and every chapter opens with a box naming the neighbouring chapters that own adjacent material. The only strong advice: don't start chapter 02 without having read chapter 05.
791bdd90be:
Both plans allocate time roughly in proportion to exam weight. Small domains get a floor of an hour or two each. The foundations get a little extra, since every other domain depends on them.

Each content chapter is 10,000 to 23,000 words. At a careful technical reading pace, that's 1.5 to 3 hours per chapter, plus about an hour running and modifying its companion folder. The plans assume you read with the companion open and run the examples as you reach them, not afterwards.
2445146280: Week 5 is the densest, because it combines four mid-weight areas. Its chapters are also the ones whose ideas overlap most: injection appears in 17, 19 and 21, and subagent isolation in 16 and 01. Reading them together is efficient. If week 5 runs over, move chapter 20 into week 6. Hooks and secrets are 2.6% together.
26cf773a86: This plan is for someone who already builds with the Messages API. It drops the per-chapter exercises, except the ones flagged as exam-style. It runs only the companion examples whose names contain broken_vs_fixed, or that match a weak area. And it leans on chapter summaries.
04af470ef5: Each content chapter has a companion folder under /mnt/user-data/outputs/ccdvf-companion/, named NN-slug (for example 05-messages-api, 21-tool-implementation). At the time of writing, folders 01 to 21 exist, with 15 to 29 numbered examples each. Folders for chapters 22 and 23 will be added with those chapters. Every folder has the same layout:
bc98fa4e3f: Numbered examples 01_*.py, 02_*.py, ... in the order the chapter introduces them. Names containing broken_vs_fixed show the failure first and then the fix. These are the most exam-relevant.
3b14643d46: fake_client.py, an offline stand-in for anthropic.Anthropic and AsyncAnthropic. It returns objects with the same shape as real responses: content blocks with type, text, tool_use blocks with id/name/input, stop_reason, usage. It records every request in client.calls, so examples can assert on what was sent. You script it either with a list of replies in order or with a responder function (needed for parallel calls). Examples call get_client(), which returns the real SDK client only when you pass --live and ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is set.
6ae1a1cf58: run_all.sh, which runs every numbered example and prints PASS or FAIL for each. An example passes when it exits cleanly and ends with ok or a pytest "passed" line.
a0351b2537: Break the fixed version. In a broken_vs_fixed example, revert one line of the fix and predict the failure before running. The exam's wrong options are usually a fix with one important piece missing.
002da18a66: Read the requests, not just the output. Print client.calls[-1] to see exactly what the harness sent. You'll see where the system prompt sits, how a tool_result is paired with its tool_use id, and where cache_control was placed. Many questions are about request shape.
c12e5a1924: Go live sparingly. A few live runs per chapter with a cheap model (Haiku 5.5) confirm that the real API behaves as described. Scripted assertions may fail live, because real replies differ from the script. That's expected, and it is itself a lesson about non-determinism (chapter 13). Never commit a key; use an environment variable (chapter 20).
2f5f150fcd: Expect occasional drift between the companion and the live API, because parameter names and model behaviour change. When a live run disagrees with the chapter, the live API and the current docs are right. Note the difference in your own cheat sheet.
1251219db3:
Throughout the guide, the phrase check the docs marks a product detail of one of two kinds. Either it couldn't be confirmed against the documentation when the chapter was written, or it's known to change between releases. Think of an exact parameter or header name, a limit, a price, a beta flag, which models support a feature, or a default value.

Chapters 02, 03, 06, 07, 10, 11, 15 and 16 use it most. They cover the fastest-moving surfaces: Agent SDK options, files and citations, batch limits, Claude Code settings, pricing.
6fccec98a4: What the markers don't mean: they don't flag the reasoning. The mechanism is stable (why a hook is deterministic, why an MCP server is reusable, why batch suits offline work), and that's what the exam tests. Set aside one session in the final week. Use it to check the markers in your weakest chapters against the current docs at docs.claude.com.
548590697f: Model names, prices and capabilities are the facts most likely to have changed since the exam guide was written. And 5.3 explicitly tests awareness of breaking changes across releases. The lineup used throughout this guide (verified 9 October 2026; check the docs before the exam) is:
007499f3e4: Start point. Current guidance is capability-first. Get the task right on Opus 5.5, then lower effort or move to a smaller model while an evaluation still passes. The efficiency-first alternative starts on Haiku 5.5 and upgrades only where a measured gap appears. Older material, and possibly older exam items, says "start with Sonnet". Read the scenario's constraint rather than reciting a rule.
a78000497f: Thinking and effort. Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 always think. You control depth with effort, not by turning thinking off. Chapters 05 and 13 cover the thinking-related parameters and the sampling parameters that current models reject (check the docs for the exact list).
cca50c107e: Pinning. Production code pins a model ID and changes it deliberately, with an evaluation run. Behaviour and accepted parameters change between releases (chapter 10).
d59dd6ba17: Haiku 5.5 pricing. The low per-token price applies to prompts up to 100K tokens. Above that, every token is billed at a higher rate. So long-context work on Haiku can cost more than you expect (chapter 15).
88c55a67aa: Chapter examples use claude-haiku-5-5 as the small model. Where claude-haiku-4-5 still appears, it's deliberate: a legacy deployment or a migration example, not the current recommendation.
71165dcf82: Almost every item is a scenario: a team, a system, a problem, and four options that would all do something. A four-step method resolves most of them.
cc60bd7b83: Identify the domain and objective. Is this about API mechanics, an agent's control flow, a tool's interface, security, cost? Naming the objective brings to mind the small set of mechanisms that objective covers. Options from a different objective then become suspect. A question about context bloat (6.1) is rarely answered by a bigger model (5.3).
49813c3870: Decide whether the requirement must be guaranteed or only encouraged. Words like "must never", "always", "audit", "compliance", "destructive", "regardless of" ask for deterministic control: code in the harness, a hook, a permission rule, a schema check, an allow-list, human approval. Words like "tone", "prefer", "usually", "style" accept probabilistic control: prompt wording, examples, system prompt guidance. The single most common wrong answer on Anthropic exams is a prompt instruction offered where a guarantee is required. The reverse happens too: a heavy deterministic system offered where a clearer prompt would do.
04f33a89ce: Read the cost and latency constraints. "A user is waiting" points to streaming, a smaller model, fast mode, or caching the shared prefix. "Overnight", "nightly", "backfill" and "not time-sensitive" point to the Batch API. "The same long document or instructions on every call" points to prompt caching. "Lowest cost" with a simple task points down the model ladder. When a stem says nothing about cost or latency, options that optimise for them are probably distractors.
454466d7fc: Eliminate by distractor family, then choose the simplest option that meets every constraint. Anthropic's guidance consistently prefers the simplest thing that works. One call comes before a workflow, a workflow before an agent, a built-in tool before a custom one, a prompt fix before fine-tuning.
5a533d9ade: The same kinds of wrong option appear across domains. Spotting the family is faster than evaluating each option from scratch.
bd55833b99: Multiple-response items state how many options to choose. Evaluate each option on its own against the stem, rather than hunting for a set that "goes together". Two options from the same distractor family are rarely both right.
b956a3b5c4: If two options both look right, one usually meets every constraint and the other meets most of them. Find the constraint the weaker option drops (cost, reuse, a guarantee).
8f758e6f8e: Don't change an answer on review without a specific reason found in the stem. First-pass answers chosen by the method above are more reliable than second-guessing.
91afa4d120: Leave nothing blank. The guide states no penalty for a wrong answer; check the official guide to confirm.
